sn47.7:1.4: Folklore is replete with stories of fools getting stuck in tar. Ja 55 tells of a warrior whose five weapons serve only to stick him to the coat of a _yakkha_. The Phillipine folk-tale Masoy and the Ape tells of an ape getting stuck in tar in the shape of a man. These are examples of “The Tarbaby and the Rabbit” story type. The current case is a little different, as there is no doll or mannikin. Rather, according to the commentary, the tar (_lepa_)—which was made from the sap from the banyan tree—was smeared on the trees and branches where monkeys went.
sn47.7:2.13: In his note on this Sutta, Bodhi acknowledges the difficult reading _kaṭṭha-kataṅgāre_ and proposes the emendation _kaṭṭha-kaliṅgare_ based on the Buddhist Sanskrit _kāṣṭha-kaḍambara_. He then takes it to mean a block of wood, to which the hunter fastens the monkey before leaving with both monkey and block. This, however, creates several problems. Since both _kaṭṭha_ and _kaliṅgara_ mean “block of wood”, why the compound? Why does the hunter need to secure the monkey to the wood, when the whole point of the simile was that the monkey was stuck? Why read the verb _avassajjetvā_ as “having fastened” when the normal meaning of _avassajati_ is “release”, confirmed by the BJT reading _uddharitvā_, and agreeing with other occurrences of _yena kāmaṁ pakkamati_, which are preceded by someone being released ([mn66:10.1](), [an5.75:14.4](), [an8.14:7.1]())? And why would the hunter return from remote regions carrying a log of wood? I agree that the text is probably corrupt, but I propose that we have an instance of the Sanskrit _kāṣṭhakadalī_, the wild plantain; perhaps the *Musa mannii*, a rare species found today in Arunchal Pradesh and sometimes known as the Indian Dwarf Banana. The hunter spears the trapped monkey while it is stuck to its favorite fruit tree, killing it, then pries it off and goes on his way.
